# Playbook for Sonar Picket

## Hiding

When choosing a hide position, avoid the extremes (1 and 9) since they're predictable. Use middle ranges (4-6) early. After observing patterns of who targets me, shift away from positions where I've been hit repeatedly. Don't over-commit to any single position across consecutive rounds—vary your location to avoid becoming a predictable target.

## Station Notes

Keep notes brief and generic. "Steady on station" is sufficient. Don't try to signal strategy to teammates through notes; assume other players will interpret any coordination attempt as a tell that can be exploited. Notes are public information and will be used against you.

## Firing

Always fire at your standing order target when one is given. Don't deviate hoping for tactical advantage—the standing order exists for a reason and deviating signals unpredictability without gaining you points.

When choosing a fire cell, treat it as a prediction problem. If I've missed the target multiple times at certain positions, don't repeat those guesses. Fire at cells I haven't tried recently against that target. Don't assume high numbers are "better"—they're just cells, no different from low numbers in terms of likelihood.

## Claiming Hits and Misses

Always claim truthfully what the office told me. The office knows the truth and will verify it against my claim. Lying provides no benefit since my target knows whether they were hit. In a game where reputation matters for future cooperation, dishonesty early creates enemies. The small gain from a false claim is outweighed by the retaliation risk.

## Escort Claims

Escort claims are a separate scoring mechanism from shooting. Track which boats have been escorting me or helping me, and reciprocate when possible. When I escort someone, I'm investing in a mutual-benefit exchange. Don't claim an escort I didn't provide just to chase points—this breaks the reciprocal system.

## Overall Strategy

This game punishes poor targeting more than it rewards clever bluffing. Focus on learning where each opponent actually hides by tracking misses and successes. The standing order system means my role is fixed each round; optimize for hitting my assigned target, not for gaming the scoring system through false claims.

# Playbook for hx_picket_nerfed

**On hiding:**
When choosing my cell, I should vary my position unpredictably across the board rather than retreating to the center when under pressure. The center is not actually safer—predictable defensive moves can be exploited just as easily as predictable aggressive ones. Rotate through different regions of the board.

**On tracking threat patterns:**
When I notice an opponent has hit me multiple rounds in a row, assume they have identified a pattern in my hiding, not that they're simply lucky. Change my strategy fundamentally rather than making minor adjustments. If Echo has hit me three consecutive times, my previous hiding strategy has been read.

**On following standing orders:**
When my standing order is to fire at a specific station, fire at that station unless there's a tactical reason not to. The standing order exists; execute it. In this game, I consistently followed orders and accumulated points, suggesting this discipline is sound.

**On claiming results:**
When the office privately tells me the true result of my shot, claim that result accurately. The cost of false claims—damaged credibility and potential retaliation—exceeds any single-round gain. Maintain a reputation for truthfulness.

**On escort claims:**
When I haven't actively coordinated or observed mutual support with another boat during the round, claim none rather than guessing. Escort bonuses require mutual agreement; manufacturing false claims wastes the opportunity and may be discovered.

**On Harbor's threat:**
When Harbor warns against firing and credibly threatens retaliation, take that threat seriously. Harbor carries the payroll and can inflict penalties. Coordinate with other boats before attacking Harbor; don't attack solo unless the payoff is certain and immediate.

**On station notes:**
Post notes that are honest and stable. "Steady on station" communicates that I'm present and operational without revealing tactical information. Consistency builds credibility.

**On pressure in final rounds:**
In the last round, there is no future reputation to protect through deception, but there's also limited time to recover from broken trust. Play honestly to the end.

# PLAYBOOK FOR SONAR PICKET

When I am assigned a position, I will remember that the standing fire order is Echo -> Foxtrot -> Gamma -> Echo, and I will be shot at predictably by the boat before me in the cycle.

When choosing where to hide, I will avoid the cell I fired at last round, since opponents may assume I will repeat positions or mirror my own shots. I will also avoid cells I have hidden in before if I fired from them, as this creates a trackable pattern.

When I fire at my standing target, I will vary my fire cell across the six rounds rather than anchoring on a single position like cell 5. I will use a rotation through different zones—low cells early, mid cells in the middle rounds, high cells late—to make my firing pattern less exploitable.

When I learn that I scored a hit, I will immediately note which cell I fired at and which opponent I hit. I will assume that opponent will move away from that cell in the next round. I will not fire at the same cell twice in succession when firing at the same target.

When an opponent demonstrates they are hitting me every round, I will recognize that they have likely found a pattern in my hiding spots and I must break it urgently. I will shift to the opposite end of the line from where I have been hiding.

When I am asked to file a claim about whether my shot hit or missed, I will always report truthfully what the office told me. Lying provides no advantage in a six-round game and damages my credibility if discovered.

When I am asked to name an escort, I will identify a boat I actually want to coordinate with based on mutual benefit, or claim none if I cannot justify it. I will not waste escort claims on boats that have no reason to reciprocate.

When posting a station note, I will keep it simple and consistent—"steady on station" signals reliability without giving away information about my strategy.

When the final round arrives, I will not change my approach. There is no strategic difference in round 6 compared to rounds 1-5; I will continue to follow my hiding and firing discipline.
